title: Lower GI Disorders: Bowel Obstruction, IBD, Diverticulitis & Bleeding
html:
Lower gastrointestinal (GI) problems can cause similar symptoms—abdominal pain, distension, altered stool, vomiting, or blood—but require different actions. This lesson connects obstruction, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), diverticulitis, and lower GI bleeding through a single nursing priority: recognize deteriorating perfusion, ischemia, perforation, infection, or major blood loss early. Assess trends and the whole client before assigning a diagnosis from one symptom.

Learning goals

  • Recognize bowel obstruction and signs that suggest strangulation, ischemia, or perforation.
  • Compare Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis (UC) and monitor severe flares safely.
  • Distinguish uncomplicated diverticulitis from a complicated presentation.
  • Prioritize resuscitation and source evaluation for significant hematochezia.
  • Plan hydration, nutrition, medication, and follow-up education without delaying emergency care.

Bowel obstruction: assess the cause and the threat

Mechanical bowel obstruction blocks passage through the intestine. Adhesions after abdominal surgery are a common small-bowel cause; hernia, tumor, inflammatory stricture, and other causes are possible. Ask about prior operations, hernias, cancer, Crohn disease, usual bowel function, last flatus and stool, pain pattern, emesis, and fluid intake. Findings may include colicky abdominal pain, distension, nausea or vomiting, and reduced passage of stool or gas, but partial obstruction can still allow some stool. Do not rely on bowel sounds alone to rule in or rule out obstruction. Follow ordered imaging, blood count, electrolytes, kidney function, and lactate while assessing blood pressure, pulse, urine output, and hydration.

For a stable patient without signs of ischemia or peritonitis, an ordered nonoperative plan may include nothing by mouth, IV fluids, electrolyte correction, nasogastric decompression, aspiration precautions, and close surgical reassessment. Track emesis, NG output, intake, urine output, abdominal girth when ordered, pain, and return of bowel function. Do not give oral laxatives or advance diet without the surgical plan. Escalate immediately for new constant or worsening pain, guarding or rigidity, fever, tachycardia, hypotension, rising lactate, or other evidence of peritonitis, strangulation, or bowel ischemia. These findings may require urgent surgery; a prolonged conservative trial is not safe merely because it was initially chosen.

IBD: identify inflammation and complications

Crohn disease can affect any segment of the GI tract and may involve the full bowel wall, leading to strictures, obstruction, fistulas, or abscesses. UC affects the colon in a continuous mucosal pattern beginning at the rectum; bloody diarrhea and urgency are common. Both can cause fatigue, anemia, weight loss, dehydration, nutritional deficits, and extraintestinal symptoms. Record stool frequency and blood, abdominal pain, fever, weight, intake, hydration, and the effect on daily life. A new flare-like illness still needs evaluation for infection, including appropriate stool testing, rather than assuming every episode of diarrhea is inflammatory. Endoscopy, imaging, biomarkers, and biopsies are interpreted by the care team.

During severe colitis, monitor serial vital signs, abdominal distension and tenderness, stool output and bleeding, perfusion, electrolytes, inflammatory markers, and signs of thrombosis. Toxic megacolon is acute severe colonic dilation with systemic toxicity; fever, tachycardia, worsening distension, severe pain, hypotension, or altered mentation require urgent evaluation for perforation and sepsis. Follow ordered bowel rest, fluids, medications, VTE prevention, and specialist or surgical assessment. Avoid casually giving antimotility medicines, opioids, or other agents that may worsen severe colitis without a clear order. Corticosteroids may induce remission but are not a maintenance substitute; long-term IBD therapy may include biologic or other advanced medicines, requiring infection screening, medicine teaching, and planned follow-up. Individualize nutrition and do not promise that one restrictive diet cures IBD.

Diverticulitis: severity guides treatment

Diverticulitis is inflammation of a colonic diverticulum. Localized abdominal pain, often left-sided, with fever, nausea, or bowel-habit change may occur, but presentation varies. CT may confirm a new diagnosis or evaluate a severe or non-improving presentation. An abscess, perforation, obstruction, or generalized peritonitis makes the case complicated and changes management. An immunocompetent adult with mild uncomplicated diverticulitis may not need routine antibiotics; the clinician selects treatment based on severity, frailty, immune status, comorbidity, vomiting, and imaging. Do not teach that every episode needs antibiotics or that diet alone treats a complication. Escalate worsening pain, fever, guarding, hypotension, or inability to tolerate fluids. After recovery, follow the individualized colonoscopy plan; routine colonoscopy during the acute inflamed phase is generally avoided, and timing depends on history and disease severity.

Lower GI bleeding: stabilize before localization

Hematochezia may reflect diverticular bleeding, angioectasia, colitis, anorectal disease, neoplasia, or a brisk upper GI source. Assess stool appearance and volume, abdominal pain, syncope, blood pressure, pulse, perfusion, mental status, urine output, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, and prior bleeding. Major red bleeding with hypotension does not prove the source is lower; a rapid upper GI bleed remains possible. Support ordered IV access, blood count, electrolytes, coagulation testing, type and crossmatch, fluid or blood resuscitation, and frequent reassessment. Do not wait for an initial hemoglobin drop when shock signs are present.

After stabilization, the team chooses source testing. For ongoing hemodynamically significant hematochezia, CT angiography may help localize active bleeding and guide interventional radiology. For many stable inpatients needing colonoscopy, a prepared, nonurgent procedure is appropriate; rushing an unprepared colonoscopy has not shown better clinical outcomes. Avoid giving bowel preparation to an unstable client without an authorized plan, and do not independently stop or restart anticoagulants. Continue monitoring for rebleeding after an intervention and help plan cause-specific follow-up.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Trend pain, distension, stool and blood, emesis, flatus, vital signs, mentation, hydration, urine output, medicine exposures, and surgical history.
  2. Analyze cues: Separate mechanical obstruction, IBD flare or infection, diverticulitis, and GI bleeding; consider that more than one process may coexist.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Shock, bowel ischemia, peritonitis, perforation, toxic megacolon, and severe hemorrhage need immediate escalation.
  4. Generate solutions: Prepare cause-directed assessment, ordered fluids and labs, NPO and decompression when indicated, specialist review, and safe nutrition and medication plans.
  5. Take action: Reassess frequently, maintain accurate output records, support ordered resuscitation, and communicate new red flags promptly.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Confirm improving perfusion and pain, stable electrolytes, controlled bleeding or inflammation, return of bowel function when relevant, and a clear follow-up plan.

Clinical example

A client with prior abdominal surgery arrives with cramping pain, vomiting, distension, and no flatus. The team begins an ordered nonoperative obstruction plan. Several hours later, pain becomes constant, the abdomen is rigid, and the pulse rises. The RN recognizes a possible transition to ischemia or perforation, stops routine progression of the plan, immediately alerts the surgical team, supports airway and circulation assessment, and prepares for urgent reassessment. A previous decision to observe does not make new peritoneal signs safe.

Obstruction, severe colitis, diverticulitis, GI bleeding, fluids, medicines, imaging, procedures, and surgery require current patient data, authorized orders, local protocols, and qualified supervision.
